# What protects you here, and what does not

Marilou's officemate forwarded her a platform that pays a daily return on crypto deposits. Her question was the right one: how do I check whether this is legitimate?

Two regulators here publish material that helps with that question. What they publish does not do what people assume it does, and the difference is the useful part.

## The registers

Two regulators sit behind that question. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas registers Virtual Asset Service Providers: businesses that exchange, transfer or hold virtual assets on behalf of other people. The Securities and Exchange Commission registers firms offering crypto assets and services to the public as investments, and publishes advisories against those soliciting without the registration the law requires.

Which agency covers which activity has been redrawn before and will be redrawn again, so one empty search is not an answer. Search both, and if a firm tells you it is registered, ask which regulator registered it, then check that regulator's own site rather than the firm's.

Read what registration means slowly, because this is where people relax too early. It means a company is on a register and carries the obligations that come with being on it. It is not a rating, not an endorsement of anything the company sells, and not a statement that your money is safe there. A registered firm can still be a poor place to keep money, and a registered firm can still fail.

Two things follow. First, check the register itself on the regulator's own site, not the badge in the platform's footer. A badge is an image, and anyone can put an image on a page. Second, check the exact name you are dealing with. Copying the name of a registered firm, with a letter changed or a word added, is ordinary practice for the people running the fake.

## SEC advisories

The Securities and Exchange Commission publishes advisories about entities soliciting investments from the public without the registration the law requires. They are free, they sit on the SEC's own site, and you can search a name there before sending anyone anything.

Use them, and understand their timing. An advisory appears after a scheme is already operating and usually after somebody has lost money and complained. A name that is absent has not been cleared. It has only not been written about yet. The advisories are a floor, not a clearance.

## What is standing behind your balance

A peso deposit in a bank is covered by PDIC insurance, up to a limit, per depositor per bank. Crypto is not covered that way, and no equivalent fund pays you back when a crypto platform collapses.

That gap is exactly where the phrase "your funds are safe and fully protected" does its work. Printed on a company's own site, that sentence is the company's opinion of itself. Insurance is an arrangement with a third party who pays out when a named thing goes wrong. A reassuring line in an app is not one, however large the font.

So when a platform holds the keys, what you hold is a claim against a business. If that business freezes withdrawals, gets breached or fails, your route is the one you would have against any collapsed company: complaints, cases, queues, years. Chapter 2 called this custody. This is what custody is worth on the day it matters.

## The checks crypto adds

The routine for any money offer still holds here: no guaranteed return, no pressure, no paying in order to be paid. Three additions apply once a chain is involved.

**Look the company up on the regulators' own sites, not in the app.** Search both regulators' own registers for the exact company name, and search the SEC advisories for that name and for the name of whoever contacted you. Do it in your own browser, on a page you navigated to yourself.

**Confirm the person outside the channel that reached you.** If a page, a group or a message claims to speak for a company, close it and reach that company through contact details you found independently. Anybody can build a page that looks official. Nobody can answer the phone at a company that does not employ them.

**If money is going to move, move a little first.** Send an amount you could lose to prove the route works before you send an amount you could not. Read the address in full every time, because software that quietly swaps a copied address for somebody else's exists, and it is built so that the ends still match.

And the one with no exception anywhere: nobody, in any role, for any reason, needs your recovery phrase.

## If it has already happened

Nothing below moves the entry back, and anyone who tells you they can move it back is the second scam arriving.

What is still worth doing, in the first hour. Write down the transaction, the addresses on both ends and the exact times, and screenshot the chat, the profile and the page before they are deleted. If a platform that holds keys for its users sits anywhere along the route the money took, report it to that platform, because it is the only party in the story with the power to freeze anything. Report the entity to the SEC, so that the advisory exists for whoever is asked about it next month. File with the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group or the NBI Cybercrime Division, which is what turns your loss into a case against a person instead of a story. And tell whoever introduced you, because they may still be inside it and not know.

## What this actually buys you

Nothing here obliges you to hold or buy anything, and no arrangement described above turns a risk you did not want into one you ought to take.

What you walk out with is smaller and more useful than a decision. When somebody puts an offer in front of you, you know which two sites to open first, what their answers do and do not mean, and which single request ends the conversation on the spot.

lessons.title: Blockchain or a database
lessons.content_mdx:
# Blockchain or a database

Sooner or later somebody puts this in front of you. A client wants one. A job ad asks for experience with one. A group chat is certain a barangay, a school or a sari-sari store chain should be running on one. The useful skill is not building it. It is telling engineering apart from decoration.

## Where the technology genuinely earns its cost

**A record several parties keep and none of them owns.** Picture four mango exporters and a broker, each keeping their own spreadsheet of shipments, and somebody reconciling five versions every month while two of them argue about a date. If none of them will accept another's copy as the master, a shared ledger they all read and write, where entries are added rather than quietly revised, ends the argument. The gain is not speed. It is that no participant can rewrite history alone.

**Provenance, where the history is the product.** A buyer paying extra for single-origin cacao from a farm in Davao is buying the story of the beans: this farm, this harvest, this cooperative, this shipper. Each handover can be an entry that is timestamped and awkward to backdate, and the buyer can read the whole run without asking the seller for it. Read that one against the limit further down this page. A provenance record is only ever as honest as the person who scans the first box, so this is the pitch to ask hardest about at the door rather than at the ledger.

**Settlement between parties who are far apart.** A payment crossing borders normally passes through a line of intermediaries, each holding its own record and each adding a delay while the two ends wait to find out what happened. When both sides read the same ledger, the transfer is its own record.

Notice what those three have in common. In every one of them, several parties who do not fully trust each other need one record, and no single one of them can be handed the pen.

## The test

A blockchain earns its cost when no single party can be trusted to hold the record.

That is the whole test. Ask it before anything else, because a pitch that cannot answer it has nothing underneath. When one owner can be trusted with the record, an ordinary database is faster, cheaper, private, easier to hire for, and correctable.

Correctable is the one people skip. Encoding mistakes happen: a wrong price, a duplicate row, a customer's name in the wrong field. A database lets somebody fix it. A chain makes you add a correcting entry that sits beside the wrong one for good, and readers have to know to look for it. That is not a flaw in the chain. That permanence is the feature you were paying for, which is exactly why you should not pay for it on data that gets corrected every week.

Private matters too. Anything written to a public chain is readable by anyone, forever, by whoever cares to look. Payroll, medical records and customer lists are the wrong shape for that.

There is a middle shape, and any real pitch will use it. A chain does not have to be open to the world. A group of firms can run one between themselves, where only members hold copies and only members can read the entries. That answers the privacy problem and keeps what they wanted, which is that no single member can quietly rewrite the shared history.

It also gives up the thing that made an open chain hard to capture. A record kept by five firms is exactly as independent as those five firms, and if all five agree an entry should change, it changes. So when the pitch says blockchain, ask who holds the copies, and ask what happens if everyone holding one wants the same entry gone.

## The limit nobody mentions in the pitch

Chapter 1 gave you the sentence: a chain proves that an entry was written and which key wrote it, not that what it says is true. In a pitch, that limit shows up in one particular place.

Put certificates of authenticity for handbags on a chain and you prove the manufacturer's key issued each certificate. You have not proved the bag in the buyer's hands is the bag that was scanned. If a staff member scans the wrong item, or is paid to scan a fake, the chain records a fake with perfect integrity and preserves it forever.

The same holds for a diploma, a land record or a delivery receipt. The chain protects the record after it is written. Everything about whether it was true when it was written happens at the door, among people, and no ledger fixes that.

## The questions to ask when somebody pitches it

Ask these out loud, in this order. They are polite, and either way they end the conversation honestly.

- Who are the parties? If one of them can be trusted to hold the record, you want a database.
- What goes wrong today that this fixes? Ask for the incident, not the vision.
- Who writes the entries, and what stops a wrong one at the door?
- When an entry is wrong, who corrects it, and how does a reader know?
- Who pays to run this, and who maintains it in year three?
- Does this need a token at all? If one appears in a pitch about internal record keeping, ask what job it does.

Jonalyn's client owns three hardware stores and wants stock movements on a blockchain so nobody can tamper with them. One owner, three branches, one company: that is a database with proper access logs and a backup. Telling her so is worth more to her than building what she asked for.

quiz.prompt: A pinned post on a page carrying an exchange's logo announces a wallet migration and links to a site that asks you to connect your wallet and approve one transaction. Nothing on the page asks for your recovery phrase. What is the safe read of this?

options.text: Your phrase was never asked for, so a single approval cannot move anything out of the address.
Do not approve it, then disconnect the wallet from the site, which takes back what was granted.
An approval can hand standing permission over your tokens, and cancelling it takes a transaction.
Approve it with a small balance in the wallet, then move the rest across afterwards.

quiz.explanation: An approval feels safer than handing over a phrase, which is exactly why it works. It can grant another party standing permission to move tokens out of your address later, which is why this trap catches people who would never type their phrase into anything. Disconnecting a site does not take back a permission already granted: only another transaction cancels one, and that costs a fee like any other. Moving funds in later still moves them into an address someone else can reach. A page announcing a migration costs almost nothing to build, so leave it and reach the company through details you found yourself.

quiz.prompt: Lorna met someone on a dating app two months ago. There was no offer for weeks. He has since walked her through a trading platform, and a small withdrawal she tried last week reached her bank. He is now suggesting a much larger deposit. What does that withdrawal prove?

options.text: Almost nothing: paying out a little early is what makes a larger deposit feel safe.
That the platform pays out, so the only question left is the size of her deposit.
Little on its own, though money reaching her bank does show the firm is registered.
That his account is genuine, so what remains is whether she can afford to deposit.

quiz.explanation: A withdrawal that works is the cheapest thing in the whole operation to provide, and it is the step that turns a careful person into a confident one. It says nothing about where the money on the dashboard is, and it says nothing about registration either: anybody can send a bank transfer, and reaching her account is not a regulator's verdict on anything. It also says nothing about whether the man she has been talking to for two months is who he says. The two months are not evidence. The slow build is the method, and the money only has to move once.

quiz.prompt: A group chat you have been in for a year is certain about a launch that closes at midnight. Several members post screenshots of the transfers they have already made. You have the money and about an hour to decide. What is the sound move?

options.text: Send a smaller amount than planned, since the deadline leaves no time for a proper check.
Hold off tonight, then ask the members who already sent whether their withdrawals arrived.
Send it now and ask the organiser for a refund tonight if your checks turn up anything.
Let it close, and treat a deadline that removes your checking time as the answer itself.

quiz.explanation: The deadline is not a feature of the opportunity, it is the mechanism: it exists to spend the hour you would have used to check. There is no refund to ask for either, because a confirmed transfer cannot be recalled by the organiser, the chat or anyone else. Waiting a night is better than sending, but the check chosen there proves little: the people posting screenshots have money in and have not tried to take all of it out. A launch that is real tonight is still real next week.

quiz.prompt: Before funding an account with a platform that first contacted her on Facebook, Marilou wants to check whether the company is legitimate. Which check tells her something real?

options.text: The BSP registration badge and the certificate image displayed in the platform's own website footer.
The blue verification tick and the follower count on the page that first messaged her about it.
The company name searched on the regulators' own registers and the SEC advisories, in her own browser.
A short call to the support number printed in the message that invited her to join the platform.

quiz.explanation: Everything the platform shows about itself is something the platform chose to show: a badge is an image, a tick can be bought or borrowed, and a number in their message reaches whoever wrote the message. The check that carries weight is the one you run on a regulator's own site, in a tab you opened yourself, against the exact company name. Oversight here is split between the BSP and the SEC and the line between them has moved before, so one empty search is not an answer. Note what a result means: being on a register is not an endorsement, and a name absent from the advisories has not been cleared, only not written about yet.

quiz.prompt: A platform holding Jomar's coins advertises on its site that customer funds are safe and fully protected. What does that sentence actually give him?

options.text: The company's own promise, which is not insurance and not a fund that pays if it fails.
Protection equal to a bank deposit, since holding client money requires that cover.
Less than it claims, though a promise in writing still binds the company to repay him.
Coverage of his balance up to a limit, in the same way that a registered bank deposit is covered.

quiz.explanation: Insurance is an arrangement with a third party who pays out when a named thing goes wrong. A line on a company's own website is the company describing itself, and nothing turns that description into cover. Reading it as a binding promise does not help either: a promise from a company that has run out of money is a claim to join a queue with, which is exactly the position it was meant to reassure him out of. A peso bank deposit is insured up to a limit; crypto is not covered that way, and registration with a regulator does not add cover. While the platform holds the keys, what Jomar holds is a claim against a business, worth what the business is worth on the day it stops paying.

quiz.prompt: A construction supplier wants stock moved between its two warehouses recorded on a blockchain so that nobody can tamper with the figures. Both warehouses belong to the same company. What is the honest answer?

options.text: A chain fits, because stock figures are exactly the kind of history that must never change.
A database fits, since a chain cannot record movements at anything like that volume anyway.
One company owns both warehouses, so a database with access logs is the better fit here.
A chain fits once each warehouse keeper holds a key, since they can then check each other.

quiz.explanation: A blockchain earns its cost when no single party can be trusted to hold the record. One company owns both warehouses here, so there is a party who can be trusted with it, and a database with access logs and backups gives the tamper evidence being asked for while staying faster, cheaper, private and correctable. The database answer is right for the wrong reason in option b: volume is not what decides this, and picking it means the test was never applied. Handing warehouse keepers keys does not create distrust worth engineering around.

quiz.prompt: A supplier proposes a certificate of authenticity on a blockchain for every imported motorcycle part it sells, so that a buyer can check a part is genuine. The chain will prove each certificate was issued by the supplier's key. What does it still not prove?

options.text: That buyers hold wallets, so the certificates reach only people who already have keys.
That the part in the buyer's hands is the part somebody scanned and recorded.
That the supplier will not go back and edit the older entries after the parts ship.
That competitors cannot read the entries and count how many units were shipped.

quiz.explanation: A chain records that an entry was submitted and which key submitted it. Whether the entry was true when it was written is decided at the door, among people: a staff member who scans the wrong item, or who is paid to scan a counterfeit, produces a fake recorded with perfect integrity and preserved for good. Editing old entries is the thing a chain does prevent, and the wallet and privacy points are real considerations but neither one is about proof of authenticity.

quiz.prompt: You sit in on four pitches in one week. Which one describes the problem a shared chain is actually for?

options.text: A school wants student grades stored where a teacher cannot alter them after encoding.
A retailer wants its loyalty points issued as tokens so that customers can trade them.
A hospital group and three independent laboratories want one shared record of test results.
Several barangay cooperatives and a buyer need one shipment record that none of them owns.

quiz.explanation: The cooperatives and the buyer are several parties with no natural owner for the record, which is the situation a chain is built for. The hospital group and the laboratories are several parties too, which is why counting them is not the test: the group commissions the tests and can be trusted to hold the record, and patient results are private data that a shared ledger is the wrong shape for. The school has one organisation in charge, so access logs and permissions do the work better. The loyalty points still have a single issuer: turning them into tokens changes what customers can do with them, not who is trusted.

questions.prompt: Your cousin sent a transfer from a wallet he controls and then realised he typed one extra zero on the amount. It already shows several confirmations. He wants to know who he should contact to pull it back. What do you tell him?

options.text: The network can still reverse it while it is recent, so he should raise it before more blocks stack up.
Nobody can reverse it, so the only route left is asking the person who received it to send it back.
Nobody can reverse it, so he should have the wallet's support desk freeze the receiving address instead.
The receiving side can be told to refuse it, which sends the amount back to the address it came from.

questions.explanation: A confirmed transaction is a settled entry that many computers already hold. There is no operator with a reversal button, no chargeback, and no branch to walk into with a valid ID. Nothing freezes an address either: a wallet is software he used, not a party to the network, and a transfer is not something the receiving side approves or declines. What is left is a request to a human being, and if that address belongs to a stranger you have no leverage at all. This is why you check the whole address and the whole amount before you sign, not after.

questions.prompt: A client messages that your payment has been sent and shows a screenshot of his wallet. You can see the transfer on the network, but it is not in a block yet. He is asking you to send the final files now. What should you do?

options.text: The screenshot shows the transfer left his wallet, so the payment is made and the files can go.
Do not trust the screenshot. Look the transfer up on an explorer yourself, and send once you see it there.
Ask him to send it again with a higher fee, since a higher fee is what settles a transfer.
Wait for enough blocks to stack on it for the amount at stake, then send the files across.

questions.explanation: Broadcast is not settled. Looking it up yourself is the right instinct and it is not the finish line: what an explorer shows you at this point is the same request sitting in the queue, and until it is written into a block it can be replaced or simply never picked up. A screenshot proves only that a screen was shown to you. How many confirmations is enough is not a fixed number: it moves with the network and with how much you stand to lose, and the person waiting on the money is the one who decides.

questions.prompt: Your uncle set up a wallet for your mother last year, kept the sheet of twelve words at his own house, and sends her a screenshot of the balance every month. She asks you whether the wallet is hers. What is the honest answer?

options.text: It is not, because whoever can produce that phrase can rebuild the keys and move what is in it.
It is hers, since the wallet was set up in her name and the phrase is only a backup of the account.
It is hers while the balance stays small, and becomes his once the amount is worth taking.
It is not, so she should ask him for the sheet and carry on using that same wallet herself.

questions.explanation: A recovery phrase is not a backup of an account, because there is no account: those words regenerate the private keys themselves, on any device, with nobody's permission. So the wallet belongs to whoever can produce the phrase, and a monthly screenshot is a picture of a number rather than control of it. Asking for the sheet does not fix it, since he may have written the words down before handing it over and there is no way to prove he did not. The clean answer is a new wallet whose phrase has never left her hands, and a transfer into it. A relative holding it for you is a custodian with no support desk, no obligations and no records.

questions.prompt: A relief drive posts that every peso in and every peso out is recorded on a public chain, so donors can be sure nothing is misused. A friend asks whether that settles the question. What do you say?

options.text: It settles it, since a record nobody can edit cannot be used to hide a misspent donation.
It shows less than it sounds like, because entries on a public chain can be quietly revised later.
It shows which transfers happened and which keys signed them, not what was bought with them.
It settles it once the organisers publish their addresses, which is what makes a chain auditable.

questions.explanation: A chain records that an entry was written and which key authorised it, and that is a real guarantee. Doubting the claim is right and option b doubts it for a reason that is false: entries are added and never quietly revised, so the weakness is not there. What a chain cannot see is the world: whether the address the funds went to belongs to a supplier or to a cousin, whether the rice was bought, whether it reached anybody. Publishing addresses makes the movement readable, which is worth having, and it still leaves every question about the spending to be answered by people off the chain.

questions.prompt: A group chat is pushing a token described as backed one for one by pesos sitting in an account somewhere, and the person promoting it says you can confirm the backing yourself because it is all on the chain. How do you read that claim?

options.text: The chain carries the reserve as well, so anybody can confirm the pesos by reading the entries.
The chain shows the token entries only, and whether the pesos exist is a claim it cannot check.
The chain cannot confirm it, so count the supply instead and match it against the stated backing.
The supply is public, and a supply anyone can count is what makes a one for one claim verifiable.

questions.explanation: A token is a record somebody issued, and it means something only if somebody off the chain honours it. The chain can tell you how many units exist and where they moved. It cannot look inside a bank account and it cannot make anyone hand over pesos, so counting the supply tells you only what was issued: it is one half of a sum whose other half is not on the chain at all. Anything described as backed is a promise made by a company, and the promise is worth what that company is worth.

questions.prompt: Your aunt keeps her recovery phrase on one sheet of paper folded inside the purse she carries every day, and nobody else knows the sheet exists. She says that is safest because it never leaves her. What is wrong with it?

options.text: It fails both ways: one copy, and it travels in the purse she carries every day.
Little, since paper is offline and carrying it is what keeps it out of a cloud account.
It fails both ways, so a photo of the sheet kept on her phone would close the gap.
Only the loss half, so a copy typed into a note in her email would close the gap.

questions.explanation: A backup has to survive two opposite events: somebody finding it, and it disappearing. One copy in a bag that travels handles neither, so naming both failures is only half the work and the remedy is the other half. A photo syncs to a cloud account on its own, and a note in email puts the wallet behind one password, so both of those answer the loss half by widening the theft half. Copies in more than one place she controls handle both, and paper stays the right material. Then there is the part nobody wants to raise: if she dies and nobody can find that sheet, the outcome is the same as the sheet burning.

questions.prompt: A platform where your balance sits pauses withdrawals. It posts that funds are safe and an update is coming, and its community chat is full of people saying it has paused before and come back fine. How should you read your position?

options.text: Because it holds the keys, the pause protects users during heavy traffic, so the move is to wait.
Since your holdings sit at your own address, they stay visible on the chain right through the pause.
While it holds the keys, what you have is a claim on that company rather than holdings you control.
Because the notice is public it is a commitment, so the balance is protected whatever happens next.

questions.explanation: This is chapter 1 and chapter 2 meeting. If the platform holds the keys there is no address of yours to look at: your balance is a number inside that company's own system, and what you hold is a claim against it. The claim survives only as long as the company does, so a pause is where the difference stops being theoretical rather than a sign of heavy traffic. A line saying funds are safe is written by the party you would be making the claim against, and it is not insurance.

questions.prompt: A friend who has never held any crypto was given a small amount by a cousin, who set the whole thing up on his own phone. The friend asks whether he should move it into a wallet he controls or leave it where it is. What is the honest answer?

options.text: Moving it to keys he holds himself takes the company out, and leaves nothing worse behind it.
Leaving it where it is passes the risk to a registered platform, which is what registration is for.
Each choice trades one risk for another, so the sensible default is to split it evenly across both.
Each choice trades one risk for another, and deciding to hold none of it is also a real answer.

questions.explanation: Both directions cost something and neither one is the safe option. Leave the keys with a platform and you get help when you fumble, along with the risk that the company freezes, fails or is breached. Hold them yourself and no company can lose them for you, but every mistake is now yours alone and permanent. Splitting is a real arrangement for someone who has decided to hold crypto, and it is not a default: it hands him both failure modes at once for an amount he did not ask for. There is a third answer this course will not talk anyone out of: holding none is a position, and finishing this course and staying out is a legitimate result. This is education, not investment advice.

questions.prompt: You have used one receiving address for two years: client payments, a donation drive you posted about publicly, and transfers to your brother. A new client asks you where to send payment. What is the real consideration?

options.text: Anyone who ties that one address to you can then read everything it has ever done.
An address stays private in practice, since it is a long string with no name on it.
The risk is that an earlier payer could send from it, which is why addresses get retired.
There is none, because entries stop being readable once a transfer is old enough.

questions.explanation: A public chain is pseudonymous, not anonymous. The address hides your name until one thing connects it to you, and after that it hides nothing, backwards through the whole history: what you were paid, by whom, and where it went next. Nobody can spend from it without your key, so theft is not the risk here. Being read is, which is why some people keep separate addresses for separate payers.

questions.prompt: An SMS says there was a suspicious login on your wallet and links to a page for securing it. The page carries the wallet's name and design, and asks you to enter your recovery phrase to restore protection. What is the correct read?

options.text: Do not enter it, but open the link to check the domain, since a matching domain means the page is real.
No wallet and no support desk ever needs that phrase, so typing it hands the whole wallet over.
Do not enter it. Reply to the SMS and continue only if a person answers with your account details.
Enter it, since restoring protection does not move any funds out of the wallet by itself.

questions.explanation: Treat every request for a recovery phrase as fraud, with no exceptions, including one that arrives looking exactly right. Refusing to type it is the start and not the finish: a domain, a logo and a page design are the cheapest parts of the operation to copy, so a matching domain proves nothing, and a message you did not ask for cannot be verified by replying to it. The phrase hands over the wallet rather than one payment, which is why nothing about the balance makes typing it safer. If you want to know whether anything is wrong, close the message and open the app yourself.

questions.prompt: An unexpected token turns up in a wallet you control. A site says it is a reward you can claim, and claiming it means signing a transaction that lets the site move tokens on your behalf. How do you handle it?

options.text: Signing costs a small fee and moves no funds, so the worst outcome is losing that fee.
Do not sign from your main wallet. Sign from a second device, since a drain reaches only that device.
An unexpected token is harmless, so claim it and move the proceeds out straight afterwards.
One signature can hand a site standing permission to move whatever that wallet holds later on.

questions.explanation: You are not being asked to send anything, which is exactly why it works. You are being asked to grant permission, and permission stays granted after you close the tab. A second device does not help, because the permission is attached to the address rather than to the phone or laptop that signed for it, and the same keys reach the same address from anywhere. The wallet can be emptied minutes later or weeks later, and because the draining transfer carries your own signature it looks entirely ordinary on the chain. Taking a permission back needs another transaction and another fee. Nothing that arrives unasked in a wallet is worth the tap it takes to claim it.

questions.prompt: An acquaintance paid a release fee to withdraw a balance a platform had been showing him, and nothing came out. A stranger has now replied to his public post offering to trace and recover the money for a fee paid up front. What do you tell him?

options.text: Both fees are the same crime, so report it and treat anyone wanting money up front as the second wave.
Pay the recovery fee only, since it is small against the balance and the first fee is gone regardless.
Ask the recoverer to do the work first and take a cut of whatever he manages to bring back.
Pay nothing more, and ask the platform to reverse the release fee on the chain instead.

questions.explanation: Money that will not come out until you put more in is not stuck, it is gone, and the fee was the actual product. The offer that follows a public post about a loss is the same crime finding him a second time, because somebody who has lost money and said so is the cheapest lead there is. Asking for payment on results sounds careful and changes nothing: nobody can move a confirmed entry, so there is no work to be paid for either way. Nor can the platform reverse anything on the chain, since a confirmed transfer is settled and the platform is not the network. What is worth doing is writing down the transaction and the addresses, screenshotting everything before it is deleted, reporting the entity to the SEC, and filing with the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group or the NBI Cybercrime Division.

questions.prompt: A representative reached you on a messaging app about a platform you had not heard of. You look the firm up yourself and it really does appear on a regulator's own published register. He points at that and repeats the offer: a fixed monthly return, funded this week. What does the register result settle?

options.text: The platform's honesty, since a regulator would not put a firm running a scheme on its register.
Nothing whatever, because a register only lists the firms that applied for it and paid the fee.
The safety of the deposit, since a registered firm has to cover client money the way a bank does.
That the firm carries a registered firm's obligations, and nothing at all about a fixed return.

questions.explanation: Checking on the regulator's own site was the right move, and it answers a narrower question than it feels like it answers. Registration means a firm is on a register and carries the obligations that come with being on it. It is not a rating, not an endorsement of anything the firm sells, and not a statement that your money is safe there, so it is not nothing either. Registered firms can still be poor places to keep money and can still fail. Two regulators publish material here, the BSP and the SEC, and the line between them has moved before, so ask which one registered the firm and check that one. A fixed monthly return is the claim to look at now, and crypto is not covered the way a PDIC-insured peso deposit is.

questions.prompt: A courier company wants every proof-of-delivery photo and timestamp written to a blockchain so that riders cannot alter them afterwards. One company employs every rider and owns every record. What is the honest answer?

options.text: A chain fits, since each rider keeps a copy and no rider can quietly alter another's records.
One company owns the records, so a database with proper access logs does this better.
A database fits, because a chain has no way to carry photographs of any kind in the first place.
A chain fits, since the riders and the company are separate parties with different interests.

questions.explanation: A blockchain earns its cost when no single party can be trusted to hold the record. Here one company employs the riders and owns the record, so the expensive part buys nothing that access logs, restricted permissions and backups do not already give it. Option c reaches the same recommendation from a reason that is not true, which means the test was never applied. Employing somebody is not the untrusting-parties case either: riders answer to the company, so there is a natural owner. A database is also private, quick to query, and correctable when a rider uploads the wrong photo, which happens. What stops a false entry is the check at the door, not the ledger it lands in.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy chain proposes recording each box of imported medicine from importer to branch shelf, so that a buyer can check the box in front of them is not counterfeit. The owner asks whether this is what a blockchain is for. What is the honest answer?

options.text: No, because a history shared between separate companies is not something a chain carries.
Yes fully, since an entry on the chain establishes that the box is the genuine article.
Yes in shape, though the record is only ever as honest as whoever scans the first box in.
Yes, provided every buyer runs a node, which is the part that makes an entry trustworthy.

questions.explanation: Several companies who do not answer to each other, sharing one history that none of them can quietly rewrite, is one of the honest uses. The limit is the one from chapter 1. A chain cannot check whether what was written into it is true, so if a counterfeit box is scanned in at the start, or a real code is copied onto a second box, the chain now carries a permanent and verifiable record of a lie. Ask who writes the first entry, and what stops them writing a false one.
